TIMESTRAL-209M · CONFIDENCE CALIBRATION · DATA THROUGH 19 OCTOBER 2026

What does confidence mean?

Confidence means the estimated probability that the proposed trade earns positive next-bar P&L after the costs used here. It is measured separately at 1×, 2× and 3× exposure. It is different from the probability that price merely moves in the predicted direction. A 70% estimate should correspond to roughly 70 profitable trades per 100 comparable later calls; it is not a 70% return or a guarantee of profit.

How we measure it

  1. Read the forecast distribution. Feed the last 250 closes to the pinned 209M model. Its 21 next-close quantiles define an approximate price CDF. The median chooses long or short.
  2. Find the break-even price. Include entry and exit fees, financing above 1×, and short borrow. For a long, raw profit confidence is the probability above that price; for a short, it is the probability below it.
  3. Calibrate using earlier outcomes. The preceding 300 forecast origins supply proposed trades at all three exposure levels. Fit a monotone sigmoid between raw scores and realized profitable outcomes, giving each origin total weight one. Center and regularize the map; clamp later scores to the observed calibration range.
  4. Freeze and test. The map is frozen before the 200 later opportunities. Those outcomes never fit the map or alter the thresholds. Reliability curves compare predicted probabilities with realized profit frequencies; Brier score and log loss assess probability quality against both raw scores and a constant historical rate.
raw long confidence = 1 − F(break-even price)
raw short confidence = F(break-even price)
calibrated confidence = sigmoid(a × centered log-odds(raw confidence) + b)

Example: a price of 100 with a 0.10% fee on each fill needs a next price above about 100.20 to make a long trade profitable at 1×. If the forecast puts only 15% probability above that threshold, raw profit confidence is 15%, even if the probability of any upward move is above 50%.

Outside the 1st–99th percentile forecast grid, use boundary scores rather than inventing tail forecasts. A winning-trade probability also says nothing by itself about the size of wins versus losses.

How confidence controls skipping and exposure

ActionRequired calibrated profit probability at that exposure
3×At least 70%
2×At least 60%, if 3× does not qualify
1×At least 55%, if higher levels do not qualify
SkipNo level qualifies, or the median forecast is unchanged

The policy chooses the highest qualifying level. Higher exposure faces its own financing-adjusted break-even threshold. Every accepted position closes at the next quote. Cash earns zero interest.

Did calibration measure confidence more accurately?

Calibrated Brier scores improve over raw scores in 4/9 cases and over the constant historical profit rate in 6/9. Lower scores are better. Improvements against raw scores can come from learning the base win rate; they do not automatically establish useful ranking or profitable trades.

Brier score is the average of (predicted probability − outcome)², where outcome is 1 for a profitable trade and 0 otherwise. A 70% call scores 0.09 when it wins and 0.49 when it loses, penalizing confident errors. Reliability bins compare mean predicted probability with the profitable fraction.

These checks use hypothetical 1× outcomes for every non-flat model proposal, including signals the policy skips. Marker labels show sample counts; error bars show 95% Wilson intervals for observed frequencies. These descriptive intervals do not adjust for serial dependence, calibration-fit or pretraining uncertainty. The yellow line is the 55% 1× gate.

If the calibrated probability stays below the gate, the strategy remains in cash. A flat cash curve indicates abstention and preservation of nominal capital, not evidence that the model predicted returns well.

Costs, timing and exact records

Per-fill cost assumptions are unchanged: Reliance 0.10%, SPY 0.05%, EUR/USD 0.02%. Annual financing is 8% on actual exposure above 1×; annual borrow is 3% on short notional. Charges use elapsed calendar time, including overnight and weekend gaps. Entry fees reduce investable equity. Actual broker terms and FX carry are not supplied by Yahoo.

As in the previous report, these are ideal close-to-next-close paper fills, with no inference or execution latency. Daily prices are retrospectively adjusted, hourly session-end bars can be shorter, and missing prices are not filled. Model pretraining overlap remains unknown. The thresholds and calibration design were recorded before evaluating these outcomes.
